quick_notes.title: Evolution of PRIs
quick_notes.detail: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957 - 3 tier). Ashok Mehta (1977 - 2 tier). GVK Rao (1985). L.M. Singhvi (1986 - Constitutional status).
quick_notes.explanation: The evolution of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), which are local self-government bodies in rural India, began with the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee in 1957. This committee recommended a three-tier system of local governance, meaning panchayats at the village, block, and district levels. In 1977, the Ashok Mehta Committee suggested a two-tier system instead, with panchayats only at the village and district levels. The G.V.K. Rao Committee in 1985 reviewed the working of PRIs and recommended that they be strengthened as units of local planning and development. Finally, the L.M. Singhvi Committee in 1986 proposed that PRIs be given constitutional status, meaning they should be formally recognized and protected by the Constitution of India. This recommendation eventually led to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment in 1992, which made PRIs a permanent part of India's governance structure.

quick_notes.title: 73rd & 74th Amendments (1992)
quick_notes.detail: 73rd (Panchayats - Part IX, Art 243-243O, 11th Sch). 74th (Municipalities - Part IXA, Art 243P-243ZG, 12th Sch).
quick_notes.explanation: The 73rd and 74th Amendments, passed in 1992, are changes to the Indian Constitution that created a formal three-tier system of local government. The 73rd Amendment deals with Panchayats, which are rural local bodies, by adding Part IX (a new section of the Constitution) containing Articles 243 to 243O, and the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 subjects that Panchayats can manage, such as agriculture and drinking water.

quick_notes.title: TN Panchayat Raj Act 1994
quick_notes.detail: 3-tier system: Village (Gram), Block (Union), District (Zilla). Reservation for women (50% in TN).
quick_notes.explanation: The Tamil Nadu Panchayat Raj Act of 1994 created a three-tier system of local self-government in rural areas. The first and lowest level is the Gram Panchayat, which governs a single village. The second level is the Union Panchayat, also called the Block Panchayat, which covers a group of villages within a block. The third and highest level is the Zilla Panchayat, also called the District Panchayat, which covers an entire district. The Act also provides for reservation, meaning that a certain percentage of seats in these panchayats are set aside for women. In Tamil Nadu, the reservation for women is 50 percent, so half of all elected seats in village, block, and district panchayats are reserved for women.

quick_notes.title: State Election Commission
quick_notes.detail: Conducts elections for local bodies. Headed by State Election Commissioner.
quick_notes.explanation: The State Election Commission is a government body that organizes and supervises elections for local bodies, which are the local governments in villages, towns, and cities, such as village councils (called panchayats) and municipal councils. The Commission is headed by a single official called the State Election Commissioner, who is appointed by the state government to ensure these local elections are free and fair. The Commission's job includes preparing voter lists, setting election dates, and making sure all rules are followed during the voting process. This body works separately from the Election Commission of India, which handles elections for the national Parliament and state legislative assemblies.

quick_notes.title: Gram Sabha
quick_notes.detail: The only permanent unit of PRI. Meeting of all adult voters of the village. Meetings held at least 4 times a year (Jan 26, May 1, Aug 15, Oct 2).
quick_notes.explanation: Gram Sabha is a permanent body of the Panchayati Raj Institution, or PRI, which is the system of local self-government in rural India. It is a meeting of all adult voters, meaning every person aged 18 or older who lives in that village and is registered to vote. The Gram Sabha must hold meetings at least four times every year, specifically on January 26, May 1, August 15, and October 2. These dates are chosen because they are national holidays or important days, making it easier for villagers to attend. The main purpose of the Gram Sabha is to let every adult in the village directly discuss and decide on local issues, such as development plans and the use of village funds.
